semicircular.intuition: Famous in random matrix theory: the eigenvalues of a large random symmetric matrix, properly rescaled, pile up into this exact semicircular shape (Wigner's semicircle law) -- a strikingly universal pattern that appears regardless of the details of how the random matrix was built.
semicircular.kid_story: A kid builds a big grid of dominoes tied together with random-strength springs and measures the natural 'wobble frequencies' of the whole connected system. Plot enough of those frequencies and they trace out a perfect semicircle, no matter the fine details of the springs.
semicircular.kid_question: What's the probability a randomly chosen wobble frequency falls between -0.5 and 0.5?
use_cases: Random matrix theory: eigenvalue distribution (Wigner's semicircle law)
Nuclear physics energy-level spacing statistics
semicircular.code:
dist = stats.semicircular()
print('P(-0.5 < X < 0.5):', round(dist.cdf(0.5) - dist.cdf(-0.5), 4))
print('variance:', round(dist.var(), 4))

params.name: a
params.desc: skewness parameter, -1 < a < 1

skewcauchy.intuition: This stretches one side of the notoriously wild, mean-less Cauchy distribution more than the other, still keeping the classic Cauchy's extreme unpredictability but adding asymmetry -- useful for robust statistics when outliers are expected but not expected to be symmetric.
skewcauchy.kid_story: A weather vane sometimes gets stuck and swings wildly in gusty wind, but a nearby wall makes it more likely to swing extra far to one particular side than the other, so its wild swings are Cauchy-like but lopsided.
skewcauchy.kid_question: What's the probability the vane's reading exceeds 3 on the favored side?
use_cases: Robust statistics with asymmetric heavy-tailed outlier modeling
Financial modeling of skewed, extreme return distributions
skewcauchy.code:
dist = stats.skewcauchy(a=0.5)
print('P(X > 3):', round(dist.sf(3), 4))
print('median:', round(dist.median(), 4))

params.name: a
params.desc: skewness parameter (0 recovers the ordinary normal distribution)

skewnorm.intuition: Skew-normal takes the familiar bell curve and tilts it, letting one tail stretch out further than the other while keeping most of the normal distribution's convenient mathematics -- exactly what you want when data is roughly bell-shaped but has a noticeable lean.
skewnorm.kid_story: A kid measures how many minutes late the school bus is each morning. It's almost never early, occasionally exactly on time, and most often just a couple minutes late -- but some mornings it's dramatically late, giving the timing a distinct rightward lean.
skewnorm.kid_question: What's the probability the bus is more than 1 unit late (in standardized minutes)?
use_cases: Modeling skewed near-normal biological and physical measurements
Selection-effect modeling in econometrics and biostatistics
skewnorm.code:
dist = stats.skewnorm(a=4)
print('P(X > 1):', round(dist.sf(1), 4))
print('mean:', round(dist.mean(), 4))

params.name: k
params.desc: number of groups/samples being compared

params.name: df
params.desc: degrees of freedom for the variance estimate

studentized_range.intuition: This is the distribution of the range (max minus min) of k sample means divided by their estimated standard error -- the exact tool behind Tukey's HSD post-hoc test, which compares every pair of group means after an ANOVA without inflating the false-positive rate.
studentized_range.kid_story: A science class splits into 3 teams to grow plants under different lights, then compares the tallest team's average against the shortest team's average. This distribution tells you how big that gap needs to be before it's more than what random luck alone would explain.
studentized_range.kid_question: What's the probability the range between the tallest and shortest team averages exceeds 4 (in standardized units)?
use_cases: Tukey's HSD post-hoc multiple comparison test after ANOVA
Quality control range-chart statistical process control
studentized_range.code:
dist = stats.studentized_range(k=3, df=10)
print('P(range > 4):', round(dist.sf(4), 4))
print('mean range:', round(dist.mean(), 4))

params.name: c
params.desc: start of the flat plateau, as a fraction of the support

params.name: d
params.desc: end of the flat plateau, as a fraction of the support

trapezoid.formula: f(x;c,d) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{2x}{c(d-c+1)}, & 0 \le x < c \\[6pt] \dfrac{2}{d-c+1}, & c \le x < d \\[6pt] \dfrac{2(1-x)}{(1-d)(d-c+1)}, & d \le x \le 1 \end{cases}
trapezoid.intuition: A ramp up, a flat plateau, then a ramp down -- trapezoidal is the natural choice when you're confident a quantity lies somewhere in a central 'most likely' range but want to allow gradually tapering probability toward the edges, a common expert-elicitation shape in risk analysis.
trapezoid.kid_story: A kid guesses how long a movie will take to finish loading: it's very unlikely to load instantly or take forever, and there's one central stretch of time (the plateau) where it's equally likely to finish at any moment.
trapezoid.kid_question: What's the probability the movie finishes loading during the flat 'most likely' plateau, between x=0.3 and x=0.7?
use_cases: Risk analysis and expert-elicited uncertainty modeling (project scheduling)
Fuzzy logic membership function construction
trapezoid.code:
dist = stats.trapezoid(c=0.3, d=0.7)
print('P(0.3 < X < 0.7):', round(dist.cdf(0.7) - dist.cdf(0.3), 4))
print('mean:', round(dist.mean(), 4))

params.name: c
params.desc: location of the peak, as a fraction of the support

triang.intuition: The simplest possible 'best guess plus a range' distribution: given only a minimum, maximum, and single most-likely value, the triangular distribution is the natural shape to draw between them, which is why it's a staple of project-planning and simulation software.
triang.kid_story: A kid estimates how long it'll take to finish a jigsaw puzzle: it definitely won't be done in 5 minutes, definitely won't take 3 hours, and their best single guess is right around 45 minutes -- so the probability ramps up to that guess and back down.
triang.kid_question: What's the probability the puzzle takes less time than the peak guess (X < 0.5)?
use_cases: Project management time/cost estimation (PERT-style triangular estimates)
Monte Carlo simulation input when only min/max/mode are known
triang.code:
dist = stats.triang(c=0.5)
print('P(X < 0.5):', round(dist.cdf(0.5), 4))
print('mean:', round(dist.mean(), 4))

params.name: b
params.desc: upper truncation point (in units of the scale)

truncexpon.intuition: An exponential distribution that's been given a hard ceiling -- useful whenever a naturally exponential wait time or lifetime is physically capped, such as a lightbulb that's guaranteed to be replaced during scheduled maintenance before it can burn out naturally.
truncexpon.kid_story: A kid's phone battery drains following an exponential-like pattern, but the kid always plugs it in to recharge by bedtime (4.5 hours after unplugging it at the latest), so the battery life is never allowed to run past that cutoff.
truncexpon.kid_question: What's the probability the battery lasts longer than 3 hours (out of the capped 4.5)?
use_cases: Modeling capped/censored lifetime data in reliability engineering
Scheduled-maintenance replacement time modeling
truncexpon.code:
dist = stats.truncexpon(b=4.5)
print('P(lasts > 3 hrs):', round(dist.sf(3), 4))
print('mean lifetime:', round(dist.mean(), 4))

params.name: a
params.desc: lower truncation bound (in standard-deviation units)

params.name: b
params.desc: upper truncation bound (in standard-deviation units)

truncnorm.intuition: A normal distribution with the tails chopped off and the remaining middle rescaled to still integrate to 1 -- essential whenever you know a normally-behaved quantity has hard physical limits, like a test score that can't go below 0 or above 100.
truncnorm.kid_story: A carnival ring-toss game scores points that would naturally spread out like a bell curve, but the machine only displays scores between -2 and 2 standard deviations from average, clipping off anything wilder than that.
truncnorm.kid_question: What's the probability a displayed score falls between -1 and 1?
use_cases: Modeling physically bounded normal quantities (test scores, physical dimensions)
Bayesian priors with hard constraints on parameter ranges
truncnorm.code:
dist = stats.truncnorm(a=-2, b=2)
print('P(-1 < X < 1):', round(dist.cdf(1) - dist.cdf(-1), 4))
print('mean:', round(dist.mean(), 4))

params.name: b
params.desc: Pareto shape (tail index)

params.name: c
params.desc: upper truncation point (standardized so support is [1, c])

truncpareto.intuition: Pure Pareto distributions have an infinite upper tail, but real-world 'power law' quantities (city populations, crater sizes, word frequencies) always run into a practical ceiling -- truncated Pareto keeps the classic power-law shape while enforcing that hard upper limit.
truncpareto.kid_story: A kid catalogs the sizes of craters on the moon in a textbook. Crater sizes follow a power-law pattern where small craters vastly outnumber large ones, but the biggest crater in the book can't be bigger than the single largest one ever recorded.
truncpareto.kid_question: What's the probability a randomly chosen crater size (in these units) exceeds 5?
use_cases: Modeling power-law data with a known physical or empirical upper limit
City size, crater size, and word-frequency distributions with finite bounds
truncpareto.code:
dist = stats.truncpareto(b=2, c=10)
print('P(size > 5):', round(dist.sf(5), 4))
print('mean size:', round(dist.mean(), 4))

params.name: c
params.desc: Weibull shape parameter

params.name: a
params.desc: lower truncation bound

params.name: b
params.desc: upper truncation bound

truncweibull_min.intuition: A Weibull lifetime distribution restricted to a known observation window -- exactly what happens in a reliability study where you only get to observe failures that occur between the study's start and end dates, never before or after.
truncweibull_min.kid_story: A science teacher runs a classroom experiment tracking how long balloons stay inflated, but the experiment only runs between day 0.1 and day 3 -- any balloon that popped before or is still going after gets cut out of the data, so only failures inside that window count.
truncweibull_min.kid_question: What's the probability a recorded balloon pops before day 1.5, given it's within the observed window?
use_cases: Reliability analysis with censored/windowed observation periods
Survival analysis of failures observed only within a study window
truncweibull_min.code:
dist = stats.truncweibull_min(c=1.5, a=0.1, b=3)
print('P(X < 1.5):', round(dist.cdf(1.5), 4))
print('mean:', round(dist.mean(), 4))

params.name: lam
params.desc: shape parameter (0 gives logistic, 0.14 approximates normal, 1 gives uniform)

tukeylambda.intuition: Tukey lambda is defined by its quantile (inverse-CDF) function rather than a closed-form pdf, and a single knob lambda smoothly sweeps through shapes from heavy-tailed logistic, through something extremely close to normal (near lambda=0.14), all the way to the flat uniform distribution (lambda=1).
tukeylambda.kid_story: A toy 'shape machine' has one dial: turn it one way and the output looks like a fat-tailed logistic curve, turn it to the sweet spot and it looks almost exactly like a normal bell curve, turn it further and it flattens all the way out to a uniform block.
tukeylambda.kid_question: At the near-normal setting (lambda=0.14), what's the probability the output falls between -1 and 1?
use_cases: Flexible family for exploratory data analysis and QQ-plot shape diagnostics
Simulating data with tunable tail weight for robustness studies
tukeylambda.code:
dist = stats.tukeylambda(lam=0.14)
print('P(-1 < X < 1):', round(dist.cdf(1) - dist.cdf(-1), 4))
print('variance:', round(dist.var(), 4))

params.name: kappa
params.desc: concentration parameter (higher = tighter clustering around the mean direction)

vonmises.intuition: The 'circular normal' distribution: it plays the same role for angles and directions that the normal distribution plays for straight-line measurements, correctly wrapping around so that an angle near +pi is treated as close to an angle near -pi.
vonmises.kid_story: A kid uses a compass to note which direction a weathervane points every hour on a windy day. It mostly points in one favorite direction but wobbles around it, and because compass directions wrap around (0 and 360 degrees are the same), you need a distribution built specifically for circles.
vonmises.kid_question: What's the probability the weathervane points within 1 radian of its favorite direction?
use_cases: Directional/circular statistics for wind direction and compass bearings
Modeling phase angles in signal processing and biological rhythms
vonmises.code:
dist = stats.vonmises(kappa=3)
print('P(-1 < angle < 1):', round(dist.cdf(1) - dist.cdf(-1), 4))
print('circular mean:', round(dist.mean(), 4))

params.name: kappa
params.desc: concentration parameter (higher = tighter clustering around the mean)

vonmises_line.intuition: This uses the exact same formula as the circular von Mises distribution, but scipy treats it as an ordinary distribution on the real line (no wraparound at the edges) -- useful when you want the von Mises bump shape for a bounded linear quantity rather than a genuinely circular one.
vonmises_line.kid_story: A kid uses the same 'clustered bump' shape as the weathervane example, but this time to describe a swing's push-strength setting on a fixed dial from -pi to pi, where the two ends of the dial are treated as genuinely different, not wrapped together.
vonmises_line.kid_question: What's the probability the dial setting falls within 1 unit of its most likely value?
use_cases: Bounded-interval bump-shaped data without circular wraparound semantics
Modeling concentrated data on a fixed linear range using the von Mises shape
vonmises_line.code:
dist = stats.vonmises_line(kappa=3)
print('P(-1 < X < 1):', round(dist.cdf(1) - dist.cdf(-1), 4))
print('mean:', round(dist.mean(), 4))

wald.intuition: Wald is simply the inverse Gaussian distribution with its mean locked at exactly 1 -- a fixed reference version of the same 'first time a drifting random walk crosses a level' story, often used as a standardized building block in sequential-testing theory.
wald.kid_story: Same snail-crawling-to-the-lettuce story as inverse Gaussian, but now the lettuce is always placed at exactly the snail's typical average travel unit away, giving one fixed, standard version of the race to compare against.
wald.kid_question: What's the probability the snail reaches the lettuce within 0.8 time units?
use_cases: Sequential probability ratio testing in statistics
Standardized first-passage-time modeling in drift-diffusion processes
wald.code:
dist = stats.wald()
print('P(reaches leaf by t=0.8):', round(dist.cdf(0.8), 4))
print('mean time:', round(dist.mean(), 4))

params.name: c
params.desc: shape parameter

weibull_max.intuition: The mirror image of the ordinary (minimum) Weibull distribution, reflected onto the negative numbers -- it's the exact distribution of the maximum of many Weibull-tailed values, used whenever the quantity of interest is naturally capped from above rather than below.
weibull_max.kid_story: A kid tracks the highest score anyone gets across many rounds of a game where scores are Weibull-shaped and can never exceed a hard ceiling of 0 (measured as 'distance below the maximum possible score'), so it always comes out negative or zero.
weibull_max.kid_question: What's the probability the score is above -1 (close to the ceiling)?
use_cases: Modeling maximum values with a hard upper physical limit
Extreme value theory: minimal-strength-link reflected onto maxima
weibull_max.code:
dist = stats.weibull_max(c=1.5)
print('P(X > -1):', round(dist.sf(-1), 4))
print('mean:', round(dist.mean(), 4))

params.name: c
params.desc: shape parameter, 0 < c < 1 (higher = tighter clustering)

wrapcauchy.intuition: Take the notoriously heavy-tailed Cauchy distribution and wrap it around a circle like winding string around a spool -- the result keeps a distinctive sharply-peaked, heavy-tailed circular shape, useful for directional data with occasional wild outlier angles.
wrapcauchy.kid_story: A spinning arrow on a board mostly points in one favorite direction but every so often flings around wildly to point almost anywhere, more dramatically than the gentler von Mises weathervane would predict.
wrapcauchy.kid_question: What's the probability the arrow's angle falls within 1 radian of its favorite direction?
use_cases: Circular statistics with heavy-tailed, outlier-prone directional data
Modeling wind direction data with occasional extreme gusts
wrapcauchy.code:
import numpy as np
dist = stats.wrapcauchy(c=0.5)
p_near_zero = dist.cdf(1) + dist.sf(2*np.pi - 1)
print('P(within 1 rad of favorite dir):', round(p_near_zero, 4))
print('variance:', round(dist.var(), 4))

params.name: n
params.desc: number of trials

params.name: a
params.desc: shape parameter of the underlying Beta success-probability, alpha

params.name: b
params.desc: shape parameter of the underlying Beta success-probability, beta

betabinom.intuition: Beta-binomial is what you get when the coin you're flipping n times doesn't have a fixed known bias -- instead, its success probability is itself random, drawn from a Beta distribution -- which produces more spread-out ('overdispersed') counts than a plain binomial with a fixed p.
betabinom.kid_story: A kid visits 10 different houses trick-or-treating, and each house has its own random chance of giving out candy (some houses are more generous than others, varying randomly). The total number of houses that give candy follows a beta-binomial, not a plain binomial, because the odds themselves vary house to house.
betabinom.kid_question: What's the probability exactly 6 out of the 10 houses give candy?
use_cases: Overdispersed count data modeling in ecology and epidemiology
Bayesian A/B testing with variable per-user conversion rates
betabinom.code:
dist = stats.betabinom(n=10, a=2, b=3)
print('P(exactly 6 houses):', round(dist.pmf(6), 4))
print('expected houses:', round(dist.mean(), 4))

params.name: n
params.desc: target number of successes

params.name: a
params.desc: shape parameter of the underlying Beta success-probability, alpha

params.name: b
params.desc: shape parameter of the underlying Beta success-probability, beta

betanbinom.intuition: Just as beta-binomial adds randomness to the success probability of a binomial count, beta-negative-binomial adds that same randomness to a negative binomial -- counting the number of failures before the n-th success, where the success chance itself varies randomly.
betanbinom.kid_story: A kid keeps flipping a strange coin, collected from a jar of coins with different random biases, until they get 10 heads total. Because the coin's bias itself is a random pick from that jar, the number of tails they rack up along the way follows a beta-negative-binomial distribution.
betanbinom.kid_question: What's the probability the kid needs exactly 4 extra tails before reaching 10 heads?
use_cases: Overdispersed count/waiting-time modeling with variable success rates
Insurance claims frequency modeling with heterogeneous risk
betanbinom.code:
dist = stats.betanbinom(n=10, a=2, b=3)
print('P(exactly 4 tails):', round(dist.pmf(4), 4))
print('expected tails:', round(dist.mean(), 4))

params.name: lambda_
params.desc: decay rate parameter (higher = faster drop-off toward low values)

params.name: N
params.desc: number of possible outcome values, 0 through N-1

boltzmann.intuition: This is the discrete, truncated version of the exponential distribution -- named for the physics of energy levels in a system at thermal equilibrium, where lower energy states are exponentially more likely than higher ones, but there's only a finite number of levels available.
boltzmann.kid_story: A video game has 10 possible power-up levels a mystery box can drop, numbered 0 through 9. Low-numbered (common) power-ups drop far more often than high-numbered (rare) ones, following an exponential-style drop-off, but the box can never drop level 10 or higher because it doesn't exist.
boltzmann.kid_question: What's the probability the mystery box drops a power-up at level 2 or lower?
use_cases: Statistical mechanics: energy level occupation at thermal equilibrium
Modeling truncated exponential-decay count data with a hard maximum
boltzmann.code:
dist = stats.boltzmann(lambda_=1, N=10)
print('P(level <= 2):', round(dist.cdf(2), 4))
print('mean level:', round(dist.mean(), 4))

params.name: a
params.desc: decay rate parameter (higher = tighter clustering around zero)

dlaplace.intuition: The integer-valued cousin of the Laplace distribution: a sharp peak at zero with two symmetric, exponentially-decaying tails in both directions -- a natural model for rounding errors or integer-valued noise that's more likely to be small than large, in either direction.
dlaplace.kid_story: A kid counts how many steps off-target their beanbag toss lands, left or right of a target line drawn on the ground, only in whole-step units. Small misses (in either direction) are common, big misses get rarer and rarer symmetrically.
dlaplace.kid_question: What's the probability the beanbag lands within 2 steps of the target line, in either direction?
use_cases: Discretized noise modeling for digital signal quantization error
Integer-valued financial tick-size and rounding error modeling
dlaplace.code:
dist = stats.dlaplace(a=0.8)
print('P(|steps off| <= 2):', round(dist.cdf(2) - dist.cdf(-3), 4))
print('variance:', round(dist.var(), 4))

params.name: p
params.desc: shape parameter, 0 < p < 1

logser.intuition: The logarithmic series distribution is the classic model in ecology for 'species abundance' -- most species in a habitat are observed just once or a few times, and progressively fewer species are seen many times, matching exactly this rapidly-decaying pattern.
logser.kid_story: A kid on a nature walk tallies how many times they spot each type of bug. Most bug species get spotted just once, a fair number get spotted twice, and only a rare few super-common bugs get spotted many, many times.
logser.kid_question: What's the probability a given bug species was spotted exactly 3 times?
use_cases: Species abundance modeling in ecology (Fisher's logarithmic series)
Word-frequency and linguistic corpus modeling
logser.code:
dist = stats.logser(p=0.6)
print('P(spotted exactly 3 times):', round(dist.pmf(3), 4))
print('mean count:', round(dist.mean(), 4))

params.name: M
params.desc: total number of objects in the bin

params.name: n
params.desc: number of Type I objects in the bin

params.name: N
params.desc: number of objects drawn (as a single handful)

params.name: odds
params.desc: odds ratio favoring Type I objects being drawn

nchypergeom_fisher.intuition: Ordinary hypergeometric assumes every object is equally likely to be drawn, but Fisher's noncentral version adds a bias (the odds ratio) favoring one type over the other -- as if drawing a whole handful of biased marbles from a bag at once, all in one grab.
nchypergeom_fisher.kid_story: A jar has 7 red gumballs and 13 blue ones (20 total). A kid grabs a fistful of 12 gumballs all at once, but red gumballs are stickier and 1.5 times more likely to end up in the grab than blue ones.
nchypergeom_fisher.kid_question: What's the probability the kid's fistful contains exactly 5 red gumballs?
use_cases: Genetic association studies (biased allele sampling)
Modeling biased urn/lottery draws where one group is favored
nchypergeom_fisher.code:
dist = stats.nchypergeom_fisher(M=20, n=7, N=12, odds=1.5)
print('P(exactly 5 red):', round(dist.pmf(5), 4))
print('expected red count:', round(dist.mean(), 4))

params.name: M
params.desc: total number of objects in the bin

params.name: n
params.desc: number of Type I objects in the bin

params.name: N
params.desc: number of objects drawn (one at a time)

params.name: odds
params.desc: odds ratio favoring Type I objects being drawn

nchypergeom_wallenius.intuition: Wallenius' version models the same biased-draw idea as Fisher's, but for drawing objects one at a time (without replacement) rather than all in one handful -- the bias compounds sequentially as the pool of remaining objects shrinks, giving subtly different odds than Fisher's simultaneous-grab version.
nchypergeom_wallenius.kid_story: Same jar of 7 red and 13 blue gumballs, but now the kid picks 12 of them out one at a time, and each time a sticky red gumball is 1.5 times more likely to be grabbed next than a blue one, updating as gumballs are removed.
nchypergeom_wallenius.kid_question: What's the probability the kid ends up with exactly 5 red gumballs after picking one at a time?
use_cases: Sequential biased sampling models in ecology and genetics
Modeling sports draft/selection processes with preferential picking
nchypergeom_wallenius.code:
dist = stats.nchypergeom_wallenius(M=20, n=7, N=12, odds=1.5)
print('P(exactly 5 red):', round(dist.pmf(5), 4))
print('expected red count:', round(dist.mean(), 4))

params.name: M
params.desc: total population size

params.name: n
params.desc: number of 'success' (red) objects in the population

params.name: r
params.desc: number of 'failure' (blue) objects to wait for

nhypergeom.intuition: Like drawing marbles from a bag without replacement, but instead of stopping after a fixed number of draws, you keep drawing until you've collected a target number of 'failures' -- the negative hypergeometric counts how many 'successes' you happened to pick up along the way.
nhypergeom.kid_story: A bin has 20 socks, 7 of them are the kid's favorite striped ones. The kid pulls socks out one at a time (without putting any back) until they've pulled out 5 plain (non-striped) socks, and counts how many striped socks they happened to grab in the process.
nhypergeom.kid_question: What's the probability the kid grabbed exactly 3 striped socks along the way?
use_cases: Quality control acceptance sampling (draw until a fixed number of defects)
Ecological capture-recapture study design
nhypergeom.code:
dist = stats.nhypergeom(M=20, n=7, r=5)
print('P(exactly 3 striped):', round(dist.pmf(3), 4))
print('expected striped count:', round(dist.mean(), 4))

params.name: lambda_
params.desc: decay rate parameter (higher = faster drop-off)

planck.intuition: This is the discrete exponential distribution on all non-negative integers, named for its role in Planck's law of blackbody radiation describing how photon energy states are occupied -- it's mathematically identical to a geometric distribution, just re-parameterized in terms of a decay rate.
planck.kid_story: A vending machine dispenses a random number of extra bonus stickers with each purchase, and getting 0 extra stickers is most common, getting 1 extra is less common, and so on, dropping off at a steady exponential rate the more stickers you'd need.
planck.kid_question: What's the probability of getting exactly 2 bonus stickers?
use_cases: Blackbody radiation photon occupation number modeling in physics
Discrete waiting-time and count modeling equivalent to the geometric distribution
planck.code:
dist = stats.planck(lambda_=0.5)
print('P(exactly 2 stickers):', round(dist.pmf(2), 4))
print('mean stickers:', round(dist.mean(), 4))

params.name: p
params.desc: list of individual success probabilities, one per independent trial

poisson_binom.intuition: This generalizes the binomial distribution by letting every trial have its own different success probability instead of one shared p -- exactly what happens when you sum up several different biased coins (or, for example, several different students' independent chances of passing a quiz).
poisson_binom.kid_story: A kid has 5 differently-weighted trick coins in their pocket, each with its own personal chance of landing heads (20%, 50%, 70%, 30%, and 60%). They flip all 5 once and count the total number of heads.
poisson_binom.kid_question: What's the probability exactly 3 of the 5 coins land heads?
use_cases: Election and voting outcome modeling with individually-varying voter probabilities
Reliability of systems built from non-identical independent components
poisson_binom.code:
dist = stats.poisson_binom(p=[0.2, 0.5, 0.7, 0.3, 0.6])
print('P(exactly 3 heads):', round(dist.pmf(3), 4))
print('expected heads:', round(dist.mean(), 4))

params.name: mu1
params.desc: mean of the first (positive-contributing) Poisson process

params.name: mu2
params.desc: mean of the second (negative-contributing) Poisson process

skellam.intuition: Skellam is the distribution of the difference between two independent Poisson-counted quantities -- exactly the shape you get when you subtract 'goals scored by team B' from 'goals scored by team A,' where each team's scoring follows its own Poisson process.
skellam.kid_story: Two soccer teams each score goals at their own steady average rate throughout a season of games. A kid tracks the difference in goals (team A's goals minus team B's goals) for each match, which follows the Skellam distribution.
skellam.kid_question: What's the probability team A wins by exactly 2 goals?
use_cases: Sports score-difference modeling (goal difference in soccer/hockey)
Modeling count differences between two independent Poisson processes
skellam.code:
dist = stats.skellam(mu1=4, mu2=2)
print('P(win margin = 2):', round(dist.pmf(2), 4))
print('expected margin:', round(dist.mean(), 4))

params.name: alpha
params.desc: shape parameter controlling the power-law tail decay

yulesimon.intuition: Yule-Simon arises from a 'rich get richer' preferential-attachment process -- new items are more likely to join whichever category is already popular -- producing a power-law tail that famously matches the sizes of biological genera, city populations, and the popularity of web links.
yulesimon.kid_story: In a school where new kids always want to join whichever club is already the most popular, club sizes end up following the Yule-Simon distribution: most clubs stay tiny, but a few snowball into being enormous because popularity attracts even more popularity.
yulesimon.kid_question: What's the probability a randomly chosen club has exactly 3 members?
use_cases: Preferential attachment / 'rich get richer' network and popularity modeling
Word frequency and city population size-rank modeling (power-law tails)
yulesimon.code:
dist = stats.yulesimon(alpha=2.5)
print('P(exactly 3 members):', round(dist.pmf(3), 4))
print('mean club size:', round(dist.mean(), 4))

params.name: a
params.desc: shape parameter (tail exponent), a > 1

zipf.intuition: Zipf's distribution is the discrete power law behind Zipf's law: the most common word in a language is used roughly twice as often as the second-most-common, three times as often as the third, and so on -- rank-1 items dominate, and popularity drops off fast but with a long tail.
zipf.kid_story: A kid counts how often each word appears in their favorite book. The word 'the' shows up constantly, the next most common word shows up about half as often, and so on down a long tail of words that barely appear at all.
zipf.kid_question: What's the probability a randomly picked word instance is the single most common word (rank 1)?
use_cases: Word frequency modeling in linguistics and natural language processing (Zipf's law)
City population rank-size distribution modeling
zipf.code:
dist = stats.zipf(a=2.5)
print('P(rank = 1):', round(dist.pmf(1), 4))
print('P(rank <= 5):', round(dist.cdf(5), 4))

params.name: a
params.desc: shape parameter (tail exponent), a >= 0

params.name: n
params.desc: number of distinct ranks (finite vocabulary size)

zipfian.intuition: Zipfian is the finite-vocabulary version of the Zipf distribution -- instead of an infinite list of ranks, there are only n possible ranks (like the n most common words in a specific book), which matters when a=1 doesn't even work for infinite Zipf but works perfectly well here.
zipfian.kid_story: A kid's picture book only has 10 distinct words total. Some words (like 'the' and 'cat') repeat constantly while others barely show up, following the same rank-based power-law pattern as Zipf's law but capped at exactly 10 possible words.
zipfian.kid_question: What's the probability a randomly picked word instance is one of the top-3 most common words?
use_cases: Word frequency modeling for finite vocabularies (limited corpora)
Recommendation system and catalog popularity modeling with a fixed item count
zipfian.code:
dist = stats.zipfian(a=1.2, n=10)
print('P(rank <= 3):', round(dist.cdf(3), 4))
print('mean rank:', round(dist.mean(), 4))
